passage: Okay, Urmila, Sumit here, you asked how I got through the placement interview, so here's the strange part. I sat down, the panel started introducing themselves, and my heart was going like a drum. So I pressed all ten fingers flat on the table and spread them wide, like I was holding the wood down. It felt solid. My breathing slowed a little. One interviewer glanced at my hands and I thought, great, now they think I'm bored. But when they asked about my project I answered properly, and the interviewer nodded. Afterwards I told them I'd been steadying myself, and they laughed and said they'd assumed I was just being careful with the table.

qa.q: What did Sumit press flat on the table during the interview?
qa.a: Sumit pressed all ten fingers flat on the table and spread them wide.

qa.q: Why did Sumit spread and press the fingers on the table?
qa.a: Sumit was steadying nerves: the heart was going like a drum, and the breathing slowed once the fingers held the wood down. To an onlooker it could have looked like boredom, which Sumit briefly feared.

qa.q: What could an interviewer do if a candidate keeps pressing hands on the table?
qa.a: Judge by the answers rather than the hands, and perhaps offer a friendly opening question so the candidate can settle.

qa.q: How did the interviewer read the gesture in the end?
qa.a: The interviewer took it as carefulness with the table, not boredom, which shows one gesture can be read in more than one way.

grounding: A young adult presses spread fingers on a table to steady nerves and worries it looks like disinterest.

passage: Ritu here. Zubin sat at the end of our tutorial row on Thursday, and for the whole first ten minutes his hand was flat on the desk with the fingers stretched apart, pushing down. He didn't look at the board much. I figured he'd switched off, honestly, and I was a bit annoyed because he's usually the one asking questions. Then Professor Rao called on him and he answered perfectly, still pressing the desk with one hand. Later I noticed a small rubber ring in his other palm, which he turned round and round. I don't know what was going on for him. Maybe nerves about the test, maybe just how he listens. I've stopped assuming.

qa.q: What was Zubin's hand doing on the desk for the first ten minutes?
qa.a: Zubin's hand was flat on the desk with the fingers stretched apart, pushing down.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling while pressing the desk?
qa.a: Most likely Zubin was nervous or restless, and the pressing and the small rubber ring helped him stay calm. Ritu admits it could also just be how Zubin listens, so the cue is not proof.

qa.q: What could Ritu do next time she wonders whether a classmate has switched off?
qa.a: Ritu could wait to see how the classmate takes part, or ask quietly after class, instead of deciding from the hand alone.

qa.q: How did Ritu's view of Zubin change after Professor Rao called on him?
qa.a: Ritu had been a bit annoyed, thinking Zubin had switched off, but after the perfect answer Ritu became unsure of the reason and stopped assuming.

grounding: An observer sees a classmate pressing spread fingers on a desk and using a fidget ring, and considers it may be regulation, not disinterest.

passage:
Monday. In the library, Thomas rolled a small smooth stone between his fingers while Simran quizzed him on circuits for Thursday's viva. "Are you even listening?" she asked, a little sharp. "I am. The stone keeps my head quiet," he said, and answered the next question without a slip.
Thursday. Outside the viva room his palms were damp. He laid both hands flat on the bench, fingers spread wide, and pressed down until his breathing slowed. Inside, he kept the stone in his pocket and touched it once between questions.
Saturday. Simran handed him a new stone she had picked up by the river. "I thought you were bored that day," she admitted. "Turns out you were just holding on." Thomas grinned and said the viva had gone better than any of their mock rounds.

qa.q: When was Thomas's viva?
qa.a: Thomas's viva was on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he pressed his spread fingers on the bench outside the viva room?
qa.a: He was most likely nervous: his palms were damp and he pressed until his breathing slowed. It could partly be habit, but the damp palms before a viva point to nerves.

qa.q: What could Simran do the next time a friend fiddles with something while she talks?
qa.a: She could ask what it does for them before deciding they are bored, since Thomas was answering well the whole time.

qa.q: How did Simran's view of the stone change between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday she read it as not listening and sounded irritated; by Saturday she saw it as the thing that kept Thomas steady and even brought him a new one 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult steadying nerves with a fidget stone and spread fingers, which a friend first mistakes for boredom.

passage: Sit, kanna Kunal. Your cousin says your pen-clicking is rude, so let your Lakshmi Paati tell you something. When I was twenty, I went for my first teaching post interview in Madurai. Five people behind one long table. My hands were shaking so badly I could not hold the tea cup they offered. So I put my hands under the table, pressed my fingers flat and wide against the wood, and pushed. Slowly the shaking went into the table. One man on the panel kept frowning at my arms, as if I were fidgeting and not serious. But the lady at the centre listened to my answers, not my elbows. Months later, after I had joined, she told me she twisted the end of her sari during interviews for the same reason. I got the post, kanna.

qa.q: What could young Lakshmi not hold because her hands were shaking?
qa.a: She could not hold the tea cup they offered.

qa.q: What was young Lakshmi feeling before the interview, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was very anxious: her hands shook so much she could not hold a cup. It could also have been excitement, but the pressing to stop the shaking suggests nerves.

qa.q: What choice did young Lakshmi make when her hands shook, and why did it help?
qa.a: She pressed her spread fingers hard against the table, which let the shaking go into the wood so she could answer steadily.

qa.q: How might the frowning man on the panel have read Lakshmi's arms?
qa.a: He probably took the movement as fidgeting and a sign she was not serious, missing that it was helping her stay calm.

grounding: Shows a young woman quietly pressing spread fingers on a table to calm her nerves while one observer misreads it as unseriousness.

passage: The placement cell's group discussion started forty minutes late, so the panel cut it to ten minutes. A diesel generator droned outside the window. Harish sat with a silver spinner ring on his thumb, turning it round and round under the table. Jomon, the final-year student helping the panel keep notes, wrote "distracted?" beside his name. Then Harish leaned in and summed up the whole argument in three clean points, catching a figure two others had got wrong. After the session Jomon asked him about the ring. "It stops my hands from shaking when I'm put on the spot," Harish said. "Without it I go blank." Jomon looked down at his note, crossed out the word and the question mark, and wrote "clear summariser" instead.

qa.q: How long did the panel cut the group discussion to?
qa.a: The panel cut it to ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Harish's turning of the ring suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Most likely he was nervous about being on the spot, since he says the ring stops his hands shaking. Someone could read it as boredom, but his sharp summary shows he was engaged.

qa.q: What went wrong in Jomon's first note, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Jomon judged the ring as distraction too quickly; looking at what Harish actually said and then asking him about it corrected the note.

qa.q: What would change if Jomon had never asked about the ring?
qa.a: Harish might have been marked as distracted, and a habit that kept him calm could have cost him a fair score.

grounding: Shows a fidget ring helping a nervous candidate stay focused under time pressure, and an observer learning not to read it as disinterest.

passage: The placement group discussion was held in a glass cabin on the ninth floor of a Gurugram office, and the air-conditioning hummed like a warning. Madhuri set both hands flat on the table, fingers spread wide, and pressed down gently until she could feel the cool wood under every fingertip. Her breathing slowed. Across the table Neelam, another candidate, glanced at the still hands and the blank notepad and thought, She's bored. She isn't even writing anything. When the topic switched to city water shortages, Madhuri slipped a small rubber ring from her pocket and rolled it between her fingers under the table. Then she spoke: three clear points, one with a figure from her college survey. Afterwards, in the lift, Neelam asked about the ring. "It keeps me steady," Madhuri said. "Without it my mind races." Neelam nodded, a little embarrassed by her earlier guess.

qa.q: Where was the group discussion held?
qa.a: In a glass cabin on the ninth floor of a Gurugram office.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri press her spread fingers onto the table?
qa.a: She was nervous in the tense room and used the pressure to steady herself; Neelam read the stillness as boredom, but her clear points showed she was fully engaged.

qa.q: How could Neelam read cues like these more fairly next time?
qa.a: Look at what the person actually contributes, and ask, as she did in the lift, rather than deciding that spread hands or a fidget ring mean disinterest.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel once she learned what the ring was for?
qa.a: Neelam felt a little embarrassed that she had taken Madhuri's steadying habit for boredom.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using spread fingers and a fidget ring to stay calm, and an observer learning not to mistake this for disinterest.
